slot.brief: Forward-biased diode in a DC circuit: silicon diode in series/parallel with resistors (circuit diagram given); use the 0.7 V drop to find branch currents and voltage across a resistor.

stem: In the circuit shown, the silicon diode is forward biased and has a voltage drop of $0.7$ V. Find the currents in the resistor-only branch and the diode branch, respectively, and the voltage across the resistor in the diode branch.

verdicts.working: The resistor-only branch has 5 V across 1.0 kΩ, so its current is 5.0 mA. In the diode branch, the resistor has 5.0 − 0.7 = 4.3 V across it, giving 4.3 mA.

working:
$I_1=\dfrac{5.0}{1.0\times10^3}=5.0$ mA
$V_R=5.0-0.7=4.3$ V
$I_2=\dfrac{4.3}{1.0\times10^3}=4.3$ mA

Independent check: The resistor-only branch has 5 V across 1.0 kΩ, so its current is 5.0 mA. In the diode branch, the resistor has 5.0 − 0.7 = 4.3 V across it, giving 4.3 mA.
solution: The resistor-only branch has $5.0\,\text{V}$ across its $1.0\,\text{k}\Omega$ resistor, so $I_1=5.0/1000=5.0\,\text{mA}$. In the diode branch, $V_R=5.0-0.7=4.3\,\text{V}$, giving $I_2=4.3/1000=4.3\,\text{mA}$.

draft.stem: In the circuit shown, the silicon diode is forward biased and has a voltage drop of $0.7$ V. Find the currents in the resistor-only branch and the diode branch, respectively, and the voltage across the resistor in the diode branch.

figure.description: Draw two horizontal rails connected across an ideal 5.0 V DC source at the left, with the upper rail connected to the positive terminal and the lower rail to the negative terminal. Connect two vertical branches between the rails: the left branch contains a single 1.0 kΩ resistor; the right branch contains, from top to bottom, a silicon diode and a 1.0 kΩ resistor in series. Orient the diode with its anode toward the upper rail and its cathode bar toward the lower rail. Label both resistor values and the source voltage.

draft.distractor_notes: A: ignores the diode drop and treats both branches as having the full supply voltage. C: interchanges the two branch currents. D: uses the supply voltage instead of subtracting the diode drop for the series resistor.
